rule: Involve final approvers from the start; a board seeing finished work cold judges without the discarded alternatives.
Develop logo/mark concepts in black and white first; colour cannot rescue a weak form.
Match CTA directness to objective: none for awareness, seed urgency for consideration, ask after context for action, escalate across full-funnel.
Let one familiar Indian everyday scene carry the claim by juxtaposition, no headline; accept it won't travel outside that audience.
On glass/gloss, make one large dim highlight (pull lamp back from diffuser); tiny bright specks say nothing about the surface.
Only claim a position the brand will deliver in every action; a claimed position is an obligation.
Before producing, fix who it is for and what change it seeks; reject grandiose or back-rationalised answers.
Ask clients for impressions ('feels weak'), not prescriptions ('make blue darker'); keep execution with the designer.
Use telephoto compression for a flat, graphic, layered look; on people you could approach, long lenses read as predatory.
Generate copy without editing, then after a cooling gap keep A+, park A-/B+, kill the rest.
Have the guarantee come from someone the buyer knows (local seller), not a distant brand; it lifts confidence even on small buys.
Run new creative approaches as tests beside the proven ad, never as its replacement.
For a pastel look raise brightness and keep hue colourfulness; plain desaturation gives muted, not pastel.
Scope a critique backwards: the action needed after, the questions that must be answered, then which parts to present.
Build shareable content around what sharing says about the sharer; share prompts and cause appeals don't drive it.
Cut defensive reassurances ('made with real…') and asterisked offers; skeptical viewers read them as admissions.
Offer samples truly free; token charges and half-price offers kill response and lose the word 'Free'.
Make 'chaotic' layouts cohere by aligning elements to a few axes and planes; surface disorder needs hidden constraint.
Ask where and how it will be printed, and the print budget, before choosing colours.
Draw Hindu deities with soft, unmuscled bodies and tranquil faces; avoid anatomical action poses.
Lead with a face for stopping power; celebrity recognition only pays where the star is known.
When reviewing without the maker present, state the objective you assumed behind each note.
Sketch many quick directions for proof of concept before developing any; if the chosen one stalls, go back to shallow exploration.
Ask whose approval each ad is built to win; cut showbiz aimed at client or approvers rather than buyers.
Review in order: objective, elements serving it, are they effective, why; judge effects whether or not intended.
For known or relaunched products, feature the images that have since become iconic, not the original selling points.
End with an immediate-action device (code, coupon, WhatsApp number) so interested viewers don't drift off.
Get ordered depth from layering by overlapping grids at different orientations, with some elements sitting on both.
Present concepts as ideas; defer type and detail tweaks until one direction is chosen, or you'll revise several.
Rescue sterile symmetrical shots with small human or imperfect details that don't break the balance.
Put a named person (founder, maker) behind the product; a person is easier to make famous than a company.
For pan-India reach let the image carry the message with minimal text; text picks a language and cuts audience.
Light cylinders (bottles, cans, tubes) from one side with black card opposite; even light flattens them.
For awareness films open with sound, show the brand early and throughout, and make people core to the story.
Treat Indian regions like separate countries: one shared brand core, local nuance per region.
Pick brand-name type for legibility; exaggerated mood faces lose the name.
If a shot or ad needs an explanation to work, it fails; effort spent getting it is no reason to keep it.
Check that captions and supers don't redirect the picture's meaning; text overrides the image.
Mind-map and sketch many directions on paper before opening any software.
Follow up on the same argument that drew the response, and add a dated inducement against procrastination.
Never publicise how many people do the bad habit you oppose; make the desired behaviour visible instead.
Check what buyers use now; if most make it at home, sell against home-made, not against rival brands.
Outdoor/posters: one visual shock, promise shown in the picture, huge type, brand readable at distance, pure colours, max three elements.
At kickoff ask whether the client already has a design in mind, and agree how directions will be chosen.
Fix an underperforming ad at the headline/hook first; it should call out the intended buyer.
For pan-India reach let the image carry the message with minimal text; text picks a language and cuts audience.
One ad, one specific need; split a full-range brief into separate ads.
Don't over-dress the vehicle; lavish production can signal salesmanship and lower response.
Show others already choosing or devoted to it; for Indian mass audiences popularity itself is the appeal.
Treat client picks as the client's self-presentation, not proof of what customers want.
Frame choices on one clear status ladder; Indian middle-class decisions defer to accepted rankings over taste.
If the headline needs explaining, fix the headline; open body copy with the most interesting point.
Test marks at ~1 inch, in one colour, reversed on dark, printed across sizes, and upside down.
For conversion films make the product the hero and be exact and tangible; people-led stories suit awareness.
Frame offers to value-conscious buyers as risk-free (try, return, keep only if happy); choosing reads as a threat.
In taboo categories, borrow a culturally legitimate Indian heritage reference to make desire respectable.
No exclamation marks; the brand sounds desperate, not excited.
To own a category, make a memory-attribution claim ('whenever you see X, think of us') with one saturated symbol.
Don't spend part of an ad educating a new habit if a whole campaign on it wouldn't pay.
If a key label is obscured, give it room in place rather than repeating it; when in doubt, remove elements.
Own an everyday Hindi word for the category, set in Devanagari, in a real unglamorous small-town setting.
Use insider cultural shorthand (e.g. matrimonial-ad phrasing) that the target decodes instantly; it won't read outside.
Flatter people in portrait and testimonial imagery; subjects feel rebuked by unflattering 'honest' photos.
For Indian popular and devotional visuals push saturation, contrast and glowing highlights; that is the expected vernacular.
Sell wedding and festival spends on social return (face, status), everyday buys on paisa vasool value.
Don't lead with safety/prevention in India unless the ad first establishes the action-consequence link.
Prioritise expression and gesture over exact alignment, except nested symmetric geometry, which must be dead-centre.
Keep an SME brand narrow; a leader's expansion is a result of success, not its cause.
Put the brand name and the selling promise in the headline; most never read further.
When outlining text over photos, a thick halo becomes the background; check letter-vs-halo contrast.
Lead with the gain (beauty, pleasure) over prevention; people act to cure, rarely to prevent.
Aim at the large lower-middle segment; many small buyers outweigh fewer high-penetration ones in Indian demand.
Show kids as choosers only for kid-targeted low-value goods; in shared household goods show their veto.
Avoid angry, muscular Ram/deity imagery; since the late 1980s it signals political militancy.
Don't trust group reactions to packs/ads; respondents invent answers and others echo them.
Set the key sung/spoken word as the on-screen image so it works sound-off and the jingle stays attributable.
Decide upfront whether a small business needs a symbol at all; a clean logotype is often enough.
Cut relevant-but-obvious clichés (Eiffel Tower, Taj Mahal); focus the mark on one attribute.
Place the cue where the viewer can act (point of purchase/use), not just somewhere memorable.
Test whether a word or claim is understood with ~20 target people before launch.
Write a brief both sides agree; use it to settle disputes, not to refuse changes.
Agree the objective explicitly with everyone before critique, or reviewers judge against different goals.
Use the model's gaze to point at the product; converging eyelines make that spot the centre.
For B2B/industrial products skip lifestyle imagery; show the product straight with specific, detailed claims.
Never position a value variant as stripped-down or last year's model; Indian value buyers want the current thing, affordable.
For action ads, give context before the ask; don't open on the CTA.
Never publicise how many people do the bad habit you oppose; it normalises it.
Pick one attribute nobody else owns and drop the rest; don't list benefits.
Claim 'best for this person on this dimension', not generic 'better'.
For awareness films open with sound, show the brand front and centre, make people core, keep it simple.
On labelled bottles, kill label sheen by raising the light or a gobo no larger than the label.
Present and defend creative on strategy and facts the client helped author, not on creativity.
Show status products being noticed by others; in India status exists only once others register it.
Position modern products as taking over the disliked chore while keeping the valued tradition, not replacing it.
Test every claim against 'yeah, right' (add proof) and 'so what' (tie to a real want); execution fixes neither.
Don't write for a me-too product until you find a unique claim; market size is not a reason.
For flat products on same-colour backgrounds, use a translucent/backlit base or retouch, not gobo shading.
Freeze motion at the apex pause or just before arrival (food reaching mouth).
Offer the lowest-friction response route (WhatsApp, call, store); friction, not motivation, cuts response.
A small saturated-red subject can sit near a corner of a muted frame; weaker colours must sit nearer centre.
Brief audiences by explicit behaviours and needs, not demographics or decorative persona stories.
When a poster image carries details, also give the details as plain text alongside.
Grow by selling the category the brand owns, not by stretching the name.
If glasses reflect the key light, switch to broad lighting rather than raising the light.
Lead offers with the cheapest entry point; it can outsell offering the full set.
Add a small free extra to make the purchase feel complete; affluent Indians want it too.
Name local stockists in the ad; peer visibility pulls other retailers in.
In tall vertical frames stack elements bottom-to-top toward one upper peak.
In rigid categories break the category's expected pattern; the firmer the norm, the more remarkable the break.
Check text contrast against the least-contrasting part of the photo behind it.
Avoid hairline fonts for small captions; thin strokes read lower contrast than the ratio suggests.
Take the risk off the buyer, not onto them; few trusted buyers cheat.
Keep review rubrics short; many rating dimensions collapse into halo.
Put a heavily defocused coloured object behind clear/glass products to add colour without identity.
Watch behaviour and body language in testing, not self-reported feelings.
For sequels or relaunches design for what the audience now remembers, not what the original was sold on.
A campaign idea must fit in one sentence; don't take the room's enthusiasm as proof it's big.
Don't rely on shock imagery; it decays with exposure and forces escalation.
Have reviewers judge independently before discussion; unanimous sign-offs often reflect cascades.
On metal products add black cards to place dark edge reflections; in front of diffuser = hard, behind = soft.
Reject striking-but-irrelevant images that upstage the claim; clownish treatment lowers respect for the product.
Get deity iconography exactly right; an incorrect icon reads as inauspicious and is rejected.
Position at an extreme on two chosen axes; the popular axes land you in a crowded quadrant.
Sell change through status and belonging ('people like us do this'), not by proving you're right.
Avoid descriptors every rival claims ('fair', 'pure', 'best'); show outside evidence instead.
For glossy wood/lacquer, let a big source reflect on part of the surface and leave part for colour and grain.
Pair the product with an unrelated image that is analogous to its benefit; interest comes from the analogy.
Don't add a celebrity just to pass pre-tests; make sure the product, not the star, is what's remembered.
For multi-image grids, fit edges together and pick images sharing one premise.
Keep a ground/contact shadow under products; without it they float and lose depth.
Frame EMI/credit as the convenience richer people use, voiced by a relatable persona; never say 'instalments'.
Don't default to retro filmi poster style for contemporary urban audiences; it now reads dated.
Cast real, unpolished customers for testimonials; have the interviewer challenge the product so they defend it.
Choose focal length for the distance it puts you at; that distance reads as your relationship to the subject.
Tie the product to a frequent everyday cue (chai time, a weekly ritual) to be recalled more often.
Rewrite solution-briefs as a problem with conflict; ads need an opposing force, not life after purchase.
Use a soft out-of-focus foreground to make the viewer feel they are walking into the scene.
Devotional figures must look straight out at the viewer; downcast eyes don't sell.
Treat gifting/catalogue best-sellers as buyers' self-presentation, not the recipient's taste.
Ignore rejection from people the ad isn't for; widening via feedback rounds sands off the edge.
Match deity iconography to region (Lakshmi standing in north, seated in south; owl only in Bengal).
As a challenger take the colour opposite the leader, not the category's natural colour.
Use photos over illustration unless reproduction (newsprint, tiny, low-res) destroys realism; then line art wins.
Keep running a working campaign after the team is bored; repetition builds trust.
If a mark can't be described in a short phrase, it carries too many ideas.
Define 'us' tightly by identity, not by outcome ('people who already buy').
Don't pitch 'saves money' to budget buyers; it hurts pride. Show it as what discerning people choose.
Give middle-class buyers an occasion that licenses the purchase; don't sell impulse indulgence.
For shiny tins on dark surfaces the table is what the front face reflects; put a light surface under it.
Don't pitch the promise higher than the product delivers; strong response multiplies the ruin.
Write creative principles specific enough to kill ideas; avoid vague words like 'fun'.
Pick a cue frequent enough to fire but not already tied to many things (e.g. red).
